label: prose:intro-particles-as-knots
html:
The state space on which all of this lives is not free to take any shape. It is a compact Riemann surface, and its Euler characteristic \chi = 2 - 2g records its genus g. The lifting obstructions of the foundational chapters force g \geq 1; the Descartes condition \chi = -6 fixes g = 4. Among the universes satisfying that condition one surface is terminal: Bring's curve of genus four, whose automorphism group is the symmetric group S_5 (Descartes theorem; Bring's surface).

Particles are modelled as knots and links in this setting. The dictionary is a naming convention for constructions inside the model, in the way a topologist calls a particular knot "the trefoil": a loop with no crossings is the lightest, most elusive particle, the neutrino; a single over–under knot, the trefoil, is the electron; two loops linked once, the Hopf link, is the strong binding of quarks; three loops linked so that no two are directly joined, the Borromean rings, is the proton or neutron. The same objects can be read as vortex lines in a fluid, and the later chapters use both pictures.

The idea that particles are knots has a history. Helmholtz proved in 1858 that in an ideal fluid a vortex tube moves with the flow and keeps its strength [helmholtz1858], so a knotted vortex ring keeps its knot type. In 1867 William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, proposed that atoms are knotted and linked vortex rings in the ether, one knot type for each element [thomson1867vortexatoms]. Maxwell took the idea seriously and recorded Gauss's integral for the linking number of two closed curves [maxwell1873treatise2], and Tait's tables of knots, begun to give the vortex atoms a periodic table, started knot theory as a subject [tait1877knots]. The vortex atom was abandoned by about 1900 [kragh2002vortexatom], but knotted particles have returned: as knotted solitons in field theory in the work of Ludvig Faddeev and Antti J. Niemi [faddeevniemi1997], in the \mathrm{SU}_q(2) quantum-knot representation model of Robert J. Finkelstein [finkelstein2007, finkelstein2008], in the three-strand braided-ribbon preon models of Sundance Bilson-Thompson [bilson-thompson2005], of Sundance Bilson-Thompson, Fotini Markopoulou, and Lee Smolin [bilsonthompson2007], and of Sundance Bilson-Thompson, Jonathan Hackett, and Louis H. Kauffman [bilson-thompson-hackett-kauffman2009], and in Joel Avrin's band model, where the unknot and the trefoil bound the surfaces that model the elementary fermions [avrin-2012]. This paper keeps the combinatorics of that lineage — knot and braid types and the algebra of their crossings — rather than the ether or ribbon-twist preon assignments; the chapter on knots and particles gives a fuller account (Knots, Particles, and Confinement).

Two later programmes share the categorical setting without the knots. In algebraic quantum field theory in four spacetime dimensions, Sergio Doplicher, Rudolf Haag, and John E. Roberts showed that the local superselection sectors form a symmetric tensor category in which the braid group factors through the symmetric group [doplicher-haag-roberts1971], and Sergio Doplicher and John E. Roberts reconstructed a compact gauge group from that category [doplicher-roberts1989]; braided sector statistics arise in two and three spacetime dimensions in the frameworks of Klaus Fredenhagen, Karl-Henning Rehren, and Bert Schroer [fredenhagen-rehren-schroer1989] and of Jürg Fröhlich and Fabrizio Gabbiani [frohlich-gabbiani1990]. In categorical quantum mechanics, Samson Abramsky and Bob Coecke [abramsky-coecke2004] and Peter Selinger [selinger2007] formulated finite-dimensional quantum processes inside \dagger-compact closed categories, within which Bob Coecke, Dusko Pavlovic, and Jamie Vicary proved that commutative special \dagger-Frobenius algebras correspond to orthonormal bases [coecke-pavlovic-vicary2013]. Both programmes take particle masses as external parameters. This paper differs in working inside a braided category with \sigma_i^2 \neq 1 and testing whether dimensionless invariants can be read off closed braids through a Markov trace. Four scope boundaries fix what is and is not claimed: every Frobenius object used in the construction has finite rank; the proton-to-electron ratio m_{\mathfrak{p}}/m_e serves as the calibration pin that fixes the evaluation point q_0, not as a derived output; the overall magnitude of nuclear binding energies is open; and a derivation of the fermion generation count from Bring's curve is not established. How far the derived ratios agree with experiment within those boundaries is the subject of the comparison chapters.

The algebra that describes how such strands cross is the Iwahori–Hecke algebra H_n(q). Its generator \sigma_i crosses strand i over strand i+1, and the only rule beyond the braid relations is one quadratic equation,

  (\sigma_i - q)(\sigma_i + q^{-1}) = 0,

which says that a crossing has exactly two eigenvalues, q and -q^{-1}. At q = 1 the equation reads \sigma_i^2 = 1 and the algebra is the group algebra \mathbb{C}[S_n] of the symmetric group, which a first course in representation theory splits into matrix blocks, one for each irreducible representation. For n = 3 the splitting is \mathbb{C}[S_3] \cong \mathbb{C} \oplus \mathbb{C} \oplus M_2(\mathbb{C}), of total dimension six; the deformation keeps this shape.

The photon stands apart. It is not a knot but a blend of the four simplest operations,

  \gamma = 1 + \varphi_0\sigma_0 + \varphi_1\sigma_1 + \varphi_{01}\,\sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1},

the identity together with the elementary crossings \sigma_0, \sigma_1 and the pair-production vertex \sigma_0\sigma_1^{-1}. This is what lets light build matter: when two photons meet, their terms multiply out under the quadratic relation and reach every operator of a six-element basis of H_3(q) (pair production). The embeddability bound on the genus-four surface keeps the operator content at exactly that six-dimensional algebra, so the list of elementary interactions is finite.

One object recurs at the framework's hardest edges: an obstruction class, the precise measure of when local data fails to extend globally (lifting condition). In the q-deformed settings of the later chapters, questions about the smoothness of a fluid, about shortcuts in a computation and about the zeros of a zeta function are each translated into a question about a class of this kind. The translations are where the open content lies, and sharing a class does not by itself make the answers agree.
